items.title: Present Simple
items.rule: Use it for habits, routines and facts. Add -s for he, she and it.
examples: They do not work on Sunday.
items.explanation: Present simple describes what is generally true, not what is happening right now. The only tricky part is the -s ending with he, she and it.

quiz.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
quiz.explanation: He takes the -s ending.

quiz.prompt: Complete: My sister ___ tea every morning.
quiz.explanation: My sister is he/she, so the verb takes -s.

quiz.prompt: Make it a question: They live here.
quiz.explanation: Questions in present simple use do or does.

quiz.prompt: Complete: My brother ___ not eat meat.
quiz.explanation: He/she/it takes does in the negative.

items.title: Present Continuous
items.rule: Use am, is or are plus verb-ing for something happening now or around now.
examples: I am waiting for the bus.
She is studying for an exam.
items.explanation: Present continuous is for actions in progress. Compare: I work here (always) and I am working late (this week only).

quiz.prompt: Which sentence is about right now?
options: I read a book every night.
I am reading a great book.
quiz.explanation: Am reading describes now.

quiz.prompt: Complete: Be quiet, the baby ___.
quiz.explanation: The action is in progress.

quiz.prompt: Which verb is NOT normally used in the continuous?
quiz.explanation: Know is a state verb: say I know, not I am knowing.

items.title: Past Simple
items.rule: Use it for finished actions at a finished time. Regular verbs take -ed.
examples: I watched a film last night.
She went to Goa in May.
items.explanation: With a past time marker such as yesterday or last week, the verb must be past. After did and did not the verb returns to its base form.

quiz.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Yesterday I go to the market.
Yesterday I went to the market.
Yesterday I am go to market.
quiz.explanation: Yesterday needs the past form went.

quiz.prompt: Complete: I ___ not see him last week.
quiz.explanation: Did not plus base verb makes the past negative.

quiz.prompt: What is the past of buy?
quiz.explanation: Buy is irregular: bought.

quiz.prompt: Complete: Where ___ you go on holiday?
quiz.explanation: Past questions use did plus the base verb.

items.title: Talking About the Future
items.rule: Use will for decisions made now and going to for plans already made.
examples: I am going to start a course.
items.explanation: Will is a decision at the moment of speaking. Going to is a plan you already had. Timetables use present simple.

quiz.prompt: You decide right now to help. You say:
quiz.explanation: Will fits a decision made at that moment.

quiz.prompt: You booked tickets last week. You say:
options: I am going to travel on Friday.
quiz.explanation: A plan already made uses going to.

quiz.prompt: Complete: The film ___ at eight, according to the listings.
quiz.explanation: A fixed timetable uses present simple.

items.title: A, An and The
items.rule: Use a or an for one of many, and the when both speakers know which one.
examples: I go to the office by bus.
items.explanation: A and an introduce something new. The points at something specific. Many learners drop the before places such as the office and the station.

quiz.prompt: Complete: She is ___ honest person.
quiz.explanation: Honest starts with a vowel sound.

quiz.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I am going to the office.
I am going to an office now.
quiz.explanation: A known workplace takes the.

quiz.prompt: Complete: I bought ___ umbrella, but ___ umbrella broke.
quiz.explanation: New information takes an; the second mention takes the.

items.title: There Is and There Are
items.rule: Use there is for one thing and there are for more than one.
items.explanation: The verb agrees with what comes after it, not with there. Uncountable nouns such as water, furniture and advice always take there is.

quiz.prompt: Complete: ___ three rooms in my flat.
quiz.explanation: Three rooms is plural.

quiz.prompt: Complete: ___ any milk in the fridge?
quiz.explanation: Milk is uncountable.

quiz.prompt: Complete: ___ a lot of furniture in this room.
quiz.explanation: Furniture is uncountable.

items.title: Much, Many and Some
items.rule: Many and few go with things you can count; much and little go with things you cannot.
items.explanation: Some is for offers and positives; any is for questions and negatives. The common mistake is much with a countable noun: say how many people, not how much people.

quiz.prompt: Complete: ___ apples do you want?
quiz.explanation: Apples can be counted.

quiz.prompt: Complete: We do not have ___ time.
quiz.explanation: Time is uncountable.

quiz.prompt: Complete: Would you like ___ help?
quiz.explanation: Offers use some.

items.title: At, On and In for Time
items.rule: At for clock times, on for days and dates, in for months, seasons and years.
items.explanation: The pattern gets wider as the period gets longer: at a point, on a day, in a block. The exceptions worth memorising are at night, at the weekend and on Monday morning.

quiz.prompt: Complete: The film starts ___ eight.
quiz.explanation: Use at with clock times.

quiz.prompt: Complete: I have a meeting ___ Friday.
quiz.explanation: Use on with days.

quiz.prompt: Complete: My birthday is ___ May.
quiz.explanation: Use in with months.

quiz.prompt: Complete: I do not work ___ night.
quiz.explanation: At night is a fixed exception.

items.title: Comparatives and Superlatives
items.rule: Short words add -er and -est; longer words take more and most.
items.explanation: Never combine the two: more cheaper is wrong. Good and bad are irregular - better, best, worse, worst - and than is the word that follows a comparative, not then.

quiz.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
quiz.explanation: Short adjectives take -er alone.

quiz.prompt: Complete: She is ___ than her sister.
quiz.explanation: Tall is short, so taller.

quiz.prompt: Complete: It was ___ film I have ever seen.
quiz.explanation: Bad becomes worst in the superlative.

items.title: Can, Could and Should
items.rule: Can for ability and permission, could for polite requests, should for advice.
items.explanation: Modals are always followed by the base verb, with no to and no -s: she can go, never she can goes or she can to go.

quiz.prompt: Complete: She can ___ three languages.
quiz.explanation: Modals take the base verb.

quiz.prompt: Which is the most polite request?
quiz.explanation: Could is the polite form.

quiz.prompt: Complete: You look ill. You ___ go home.
quiz.explanation: Should gives advice.

items.title: Present Perfect
items.rule: Use have or has plus the past participle for experience, or for something unfinished.
items.explanation: Present perfect connects past and present. Do not use it with a finished time: say I saw him yesterday, not I have seen him yesterday.

quiz.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
quiz.explanation: Yesterday is finished time, so past simple is right.

quiz.prompt: Complete: She ___ in this company for five years.
quiz.explanation: The period continues to now.

quiz.prompt: Complete: I ___ finished, so you can have the room.
quiz.explanation: Just sits between have and the participle.

items.title: Present Perfect Continuous
items.rule: Have been plus verb-ing, for an activity that started earlier and is still going.
examples: I have been waiting for an hour.
She has been studying since June.
items.explanation: Use the simple form for a finished result and the continuous for the ongoing activity: I have read three chapters (result) versus I have been reading all morning (activity).

quiz.prompt: Complete: I ___ for two hours and I am still waiting.
quiz.explanation: The activity is ongoing.

quiz.prompt: Which emphasises the finished result?
options: I have been painting the door.
quiz.explanation: The simple form reports the completed result.

quiz.prompt: Complete: She ___ here since 2020.
quiz.explanation: Since 2020 up to now takes the perfect continuous.

items.title: Past Continuous
items.rule: Was or were plus verb-ing, for the longer action that another action interrupts.
examples: I was cooking when he called.
items.explanation: The long background action takes the continuous; the short interrupting one takes the past simple. While marks the long action, when marks the short one.

quiz.prompt: Complete: I ___ a shower when the doorbell rang.
quiz.explanation: The shower is the longer, interrupted action.

quiz.prompt: Complete: While she ___, the power went out.
quiz.explanation: While introduces the background action.

quiz.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I was seeing him yesterday at the shop.
I saw him yesterday at the shop.
quiz.explanation: A single completed event takes the past simple.

items.title: Past Perfect
items.rule: Had plus the past participle, for the earlier of two past events.
examples: The film had started when we arrived.
I had not eaten all day.
items.explanation: Only reach for it when the order matters and is not already obvious. If you tell the events in the order they happened, past simple is usually enough.

quiz.prompt: Complete: By the time we arrived, the train ___.
quiz.explanation: Leaving happened before arriving.

quiz.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I never had seen snow before that trip.
I had never seen snow before that trip.
I have never saw snow before that trip.
I never saw snow before that trip had happened.
quiz.explanation: Never sits between had and the participle.

quiz.prompt: Complete: She was hungry because she ___ breakfast.
quiz.explanation: Missing breakfast came before being hungry.

items.title: Conditionals
items.rule: If plus present, will plus base for real possibilities; if plus past, would for unreal ones.
examples: If it rains, I will stay home.
If I had more time, I would learn guitar.
If I were you, I would apply.
items.explanation: First conditional talks about a real future. Second conditional imagines something unlikely or untrue right now.

quiz.prompt: Complete: If I ___ the lottery, I would travel the world.
quiz.explanation: An imagined situation uses the past form.

quiz.prompt: Complete: If you heat water to 100 degrees, it ___.
quiz.explanation: A general fact uses present simple in both halves.

quiz.prompt: Complete: If it ___ tomorrow, we will cancel.
quiz.explanation: After if, use the present, not will.

items.title: Third Conditional and Regret
items.rule: If plus had plus participle, would have plus participle, for a past that did not happen.
examples: If I had left earlier, I would have caught it.
She would have helped if you had asked.
items.explanation: This is the grammar of regret and blame, so it comes up constantly in real speech. Both halves refer to a past that is now fixed and cannot be changed.

quiz.prompt: Complete: If I ___ known, I would have come.
quiz.explanation: The if-clause takes had plus participle.

quiz.prompt: Complete: She would have passed if she ___ harder.
quiz.explanation: Both halves are unreal past.

quiz.prompt: What does this mean: If I had seen you, I would have said hello.
options: I saw you and said hello
I did not see you and did not say hello
quiz.explanation: The third conditional describes what did not happen.

items.title: Passive Voice
items.rule: Use be plus past participle when the action matters more than who did it.
items.explanation: The passive moves the important thing to the front. Use it when the doer is unknown, obvious or unimportant.

quiz.prompt: Make it passive: Someone stole my phone.
quiz.explanation: Was plus stolen is the passive past.

quiz.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The email was sent this morning.
The email is send this morning.
quiz.explanation: The email did not send itself.

quiz.prompt: Complete: The bridge ___ built in 1890.
quiz.explanation: One bridge, past time: was built.

items.title: Reported Speech
items.rule: Move the tense one step back when you report what someone said.
examples: She told me she had finished.
items.explanation: Direct: I am tired. Reported: he said he was tired. Questions lose the question word order.

quiz.prompt: He said: I will call you. Report it.
options: He said he will call me.
He said he would call me.
quiz.explanation: Will becomes would in reported speech.

quiz.prompt: She asked: Where do you work? Report it.
options: She asked where do I work.
quiz.explanation: Reported questions use statement word order.

quiz.prompt: Choose the correct verb: He ___ me he was leaving.
quiz.explanation: Tell takes a person object; say does not.

items.title: -ing or to + verb
items.rule: Some verbs take -ing, some take to, and a few change meaning depending which.
items.explanation: Enjoy, avoid, finish, mind and suggest take -ing. Want, decide, hope, promise and agree take to. After a preposition it is always -ing: good at drawing, interested in learning.

quiz.prompt: Complete: I am looking forward to ___ you.
quiz.explanation: To is a preposition here, so -ing.

quiz.prompt: Complete: She suggested ___ a taxi.
quiz.explanation: Suggest takes -ing.

quiz.prompt: Complete: We decided ___ early.
quiz.explanation: Decide takes to plus base verb.

items.title: Used To and Would
items.rule: Used to for past habits and states that have stopped; be used to for what feels normal.
examples: I am used to the noise.
I am getting used to waking early.
items.explanation: Two different structures that look alike. Used to plus base verb is a finished past habit. Be used to plus -ing means it is familiar to you now.

quiz.prompt: Complete: I ___ live in Paris, but I moved in 2019.
quiz.explanation: A finished past habit.

quiz.prompt: Complete: I am not used to ___ so early.
quiz.explanation: Be used to takes -ing.

quiz.prompt: Which sentence is about something that still happens?
options: I used to cycle to work.
I am used to cycling to work.
I used to cycle every day.
quiz.explanation: Be used to describes a present familiarity.

items.title: Agreement Traps
items.rule: Everyone, each and neither take a singular verb; the police and people take plural.
examples: Each of them has a copy.
items.explanation: The trap is a long subject: the list of names on the form is correct - the verb agrees with list, not names. Information, advice and news are always singular.

quiz.prompt: Complete: Everyone ___ arrived.
quiz.explanation: Everyone is grammatically singular.

quiz.prompt: Complete: The police ___ investigating.
quiz.explanation: Police takes a plural verb.

quiz.prompt: Complete: The list of items ___ on your desk.
quiz.explanation: The verb agrees with list, not items.

items.title: Phrasal Verbs
items.rule: A verb plus a particle whose meaning is not the sum of the parts.
examples: Let us catch up on Friday.
items.explanation: Phrasal verbs are how English actually sounds. Learn them as whole phrases, and notice which ones can be split: turn the offer down works, but not with all verbs.

quiz.prompt: She refused the job. She ___ the job.
quiz.explanation: Turn down means refuse.

quiz.prompt: I met an old friend by chance. I ___ an old friend.
quiz.explanation: Run into means meet by chance.

quiz.prompt: The meeting was cancelled. It was ___.
quiz.explanation: Call off means cancel.

quiz.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: I looked the word in up.
quiz.explanation: A noun object can go either side; a pronoun must go in the middle.

items.title: Relative Clauses
items.rule: Use who for people, which for things and that for both, to add information.
examples: The man who called is my uncle.
The report which you sent is clear.
The flat that we saw was small.
items.explanation: Relative clauses let you join two short sentences into one adult-sounding one, which is one of the fastest ways to sound more advanced.

quiz.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The woman which helped me was kind.
The woman who helped me was kind.
The woman what helped me was kind.
The woman she helped me was kind.
quiz.explanation: Who is for people.

quiz.prompt: Join: This is the book. I told you about it.
options: This is the book that I told you about.
This is the book what I told you.
This is the book I told you about it.
This is the book which told you.
quiz.explanation: That replaces the object of the second sentence.

quiz.prompt: Which needs commas?
options: The man who lives next door is a doctor.
My father, who lives next door, is a doctor.
The book that I read was long.
The place where we met was busy.
quiz.explanation: Extra, non-defining information takes commas.

items.title: Inversion for Emphasis
items.rule: Put a negative or limiting adverb first and the subject and auxiliary swap places.
examples: Never have I seen such a mess.
Not only was he late, he forgot the file.
items.explanation: This is formal and deliberate: it signals that what follows is notable. Overusing it sounds theatrical, but recognising it matters for reading anything written.

quiz.prompt: Complete: Not only ___ late, but he also lost the keys.
quiz.explanation: Inversion follows not only.

quiz.prompt: Complete: Rarely ___ such a clear explanation.
quiz.explanation: Rarely at the front triggers inversion.

quiz.prompt: Which sentence is correctly inverted?
quiz.explanation: The auxiliary moves in front of the subject.

items.title: Hedging and Softening
items.rule: Tentative language that makes a claim or a request easier to accept.
examples: That may not be entirely accurate.
items.explanation: Direct disagreement can end a conversation. Hedging buys room to be wrong and makes the other person's retreat cheap, which is why it dominates professional English.

quiz.prompt: Which is the softest disagreement?
options: I am not sure that is quite right.
quiz.explanation: Not sure ... quite is the most hedged.

quiz.prompt: Which is the most tentative request?
options: Can you send me the file?
I was wondering whether you could send me the file.
quiz.explanation: I was wondering whether is maximally indirect.

quiz.prompt: Complete: The results ___ suggest a link, though more work is needed.
quiz.explanation: Would seem to matches the cautious second half.

items.title: Cleft Sentences
items.rule: Split a sentence to spotlight one part: it is X that..., what I need is...
examples: What surprised me was the price.
All I want is an answer.
items.explanation: The cleft moves the important element out of the middle of the sentence, where it gets lost, and into a position where the listener cannot miss it.

quiz.prompt: Emphasise Maria: Maria called yesterday.
options: It was Maria who called yesterday.
quiz.explanation: It was X who is the standard cleft.

quiz.prompt: Complete: ___ I need is more time.
quiz.explanation: What introduces the noun clause.

quiz.prompt: Which sentence emphasises the price?
options: What surprised me was the price.
quiz.explanation: The cleft puts the price in the spotlight.

items.title: Modals of Deduction
items.rule: Must, might, could and cannot express how certain you are, not what is permitted.
examples: She must be at home - her car is there.
He might have missed the train.
items.explanation: For the past, add have plus the participle: must have left, might have forgotten. Cannot is the negative of must here - not must not, which means prohibition.

quiz.prompt: Her coat is gone, so she ___ left.
quiz.explanation: Strong deduction about the past: must have left.

quiz.prompt: That ___ be her - she is abroad this week.
quiz.explanation: Cannot expresses a confident negative deduction.

quiz.prompt: I am not sure, but he ___ forgotten.
quiz.explanation: Might have signals uncertainty.

items.title: Linking an Argument
items.rule: Markers that show the reader how one idea relates to the last.
examples: That said, the alternative is worse.
items.explanation: Concession markers - admittedly, granted, that said - are what make writing sound considered rather than one-sided, because they show you have met the counterargument.

quiz.prompt: Which marker concedes a point before disagreeing?
quiz.explanation: Admittedly grants the other side something.

quiz.prompt: Complete: The plan is cheap. ___, it is slow.
quiz.explanation: That said introduces a contrast.

quiz.prompt: Which marker introduces a consequence?
quiz.explanation: Consequently signals a result.

items.title: Subjunctive and Unreal Present
items.rule: After suggest, insist, demand and it is essential, use the bare base verb.
examples: It is essential that she be informed.
I would rather you did not.
items.explanation: This survives in formal English and in fixed phrases. Note the lack of -s: he leave, not he leaves. Would rather and it is time take a past form for a present meaning.

quiz.prompt: Complete: The board insisted that he ___ immediately.
quiz.explanation: After insist that, use the base form.

quiz.prompt: Complete: I would rather you ___ that to anyone.
quiz.explanation: Would rather takes a past form for present meaning.

quiz.prompt: Complete: It is high time we ___ this properly.
quiz.explanation: It is time takes the past form.
